name: Yobe
summary_text: Yobe is one of the twelve states operating a parallel Sharia criminal-code system - its Sharia penal code took effect 26 December 2000 - and one of five states (with Kano, Bauchi, Sokoto, Zamfara) where Hisbah religious-police activity is specifically documented by the USCIRF report. Sharia courts have criminal jurisdiction for Muslims, criminalising conduct beyond the federal statute including same-sex acts between women (ta'azir penalties). No trans-specific incident or carried-out capital sentence is on record for Yobe in this dossier. Score 0.044 below the national 0.08. The combination of enacted Sharia criminal jurisdiction and documented Hisbah enforcement infrastructure justifies a deeper cut than the seven Sharia states without noted Hisbah presence. Yobe edges below Zamfara only because Hisbah is explicitly named; Zamfara's distinction is being the 2000 trigger for the whole cascade.

sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch report section on the extension of Sharia to criminal law: Zamfara's governor triggered the cascade (Establishment Law 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve states - Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara - operate Sharia criminal jurisdiction. Sharia applies only to Muslims; non-Muslims are tried in parallel common-law courts, and the state attorney general oversees both systems.

NOTE: document not retrievable at fetch time (403); the underlying USCIRF 2019 implementation study samples 173 Sharia-court cases (2017) in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara and lists Yobe among the five states with documented Hisbah religious-police activity.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on SOGIESC in Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025): the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct (up to 14 years, attempted 3 years) and is silent on women; Sharia penal codes in the 12 northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death (in a minority of states) to flogging and imprisonment; the enforcement-and-Hisbah section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and notes few secular cases reach court.
